claim: The rostromedial tegmental nucleus (RMTg) is a GABAergic afferent to midbrain dopamine (DA) neurons.
source: The rostromedial tegmental nucleus (RMTg), a GABAergic afferent to midbrain dopamine (DA) neurons, has been hypothesized to be broadly activated by aversive stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about the RMTg.

claim: RMTg neurons are broadly excited by aversive stimuli of different sensory modalities.
source: Here, we found that RMTg neurons are broadly excited by aversive stimuli of different sensory modalities and inhibited by reward-related stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: RMTg neurons are inhibited by reward-related stimuli.
source: Here, we found that RMTg neurons are broadly excited by aversive stimuli of different sensory modalities and inhibited by reward-related stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Aversive stimuli tested include visual, auditory, somatosensory and chemical aversive stimuli.
source: These stimuli include visual, auditory, somatosensory and chemical aversive stimuli, as well as "opponent" motivational states induced by removal of sustained rewarding or aversive stimuli.
evidence: This describes the types of stimuli used in the experiments.

claim: Removal of sustained rewarding or aversive stimuli induces opponent motivational states.
source: These stimuli include visual, auditory, somatosensory and chemical aversive stimuli, as well as "opponent" motivational states induced by removal of sustained rewarding or aversive stimuli.
evidence: This describes experimental manipulations and their effects.

claim: Valence-encoding RMTg neurons preferentially project to the DA-rich VTA versus other targets.
source: We further found that valence-encoding RMTg neurons preferentially project to the DA-rich VTA versus other targets, and excitotoxic RMTg lesions greatly reduce aversive stimulus-induced inhibitions in VTA neurons, particularly putative DA neurons, while also impairing conditioned place aversion to multiple aversive stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 4.

claim: Excitotoxic RMTg lesions greatly reduce aversive stimulus-induced inhibitions in VTA neurons, particularly putative DA neurons.
source: We further found that valence-encoding RMTg neurons preferentially project to the DA-rich VTA versus other targets, and excitotoxic RMTg lesions greatly reduce aversive stimulus-induced inhibitions in VTA neurons, particularly putative DA neurons, while also impairing conditioned place aversion to multiple aversive stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 5.

claim: Excitotoxic RMTg lesions impair conditioned place aversion to multiple aversive stimuli.
source: We further found that valence-encoding RMTg neurons preferentially project to the DA-rich VTA versus other targets, and excitotoxic RMTg lesions greatly reduce aversive stimulus-induced inhibitions in VTA neurons, particularly putative DA neurons, while also impairing conditioned place aversion to multiple aversive stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by behavioral data in Figure 6.

claim: The RMTg is also called the tail of the ventral tegmental area (tVTA).
source: The rostromedial tegmental nucleus (RMTg), also called the tail of the ventral tegmental area (tVTA), is a GABAergic nucleus first described in 2009 as a major inhibitory input to neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Jhou et al., 2009; Kaufling et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established nomenclature with citations.

claim: The RMTg was first described in 2009 as a major inhibitory input to neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: The rostromedial tegmental nucleus (RMTg), also called the tail of the ventral tegmental area (tVTA), is a GABAergic nucleus first described in 2009 as a major inhibitory input to neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Jhou et al., 2009; Kaufling et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: RMTg axons overwhelmingly synapse on tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) positive neurons in the VTA and substantia nigra.
source: Previous studies have shown that RMTg axons overwhelmingly synapse on tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) positive neurons in the VTA and substantia nigra, and electrical stimulation of the RMTg dramatically suppresses DA neuron firing (Balcita-Pedicino et al., 2011; Bourdy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the RMTg dramatically suppresses DA neuron firing.
source: Previous studies have shown that RMTg axons overwhelmingly synapse on tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) positive neurons in the VTA and substantia nigra, and electrical stimulation of the RMTg dramatically suppresses DA neuron firing (Balcita-Pedicino et al., 2011; Bourdy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: The RMTg plays an important role in conveying information about aversive stimuli onto VTA and substantia nigra DA neurons.
source: Subsequent studies have further suggested an important RMTg role in conveying information about aversive stimuli onto VTA and substantia nigra DA neurons and mediating behavioral responses to these aversive stimuli (Brown et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2011; Jhou et al., 2009; Jhou et al., 2013; Vento et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: The RMTg mediates behavioral responses to aversive stimuli.
source: Subsequent studies have further suggested an important RMTg role in conveying information about aversive stimuli onto VTA and substantia nigra DA neurons and mediating behavioral responses to these aversive stimuli (Brown et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2011; Jhou et al., 2009; Jhou et al., 2013; Vento et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: Most prior studies had only tested RMTg firing responses to a limited range of aversive stimuli, for example footshocks, airpuffs, and their predictive cues.
source: Most prior studies had only tested RMTg firing responses to a limited range of aversive stimuli, for example footshocks, airpuffs, and their predictive cues (Hong et al., 2011; Jhou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of prior work with citations.

claim: A recent study examined 11 distinct aversive stimuli but found that only 3 of them increased RMTg expression of the immediate-early gene c-Fos.
source: One notable exception is a recent study that examined 11 distinct aversive stimuli, but found that only 3 of them increased RMTg expression of the immediate-early gene c-Fos (Sánchez-Catalán et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as prior work with citation.

claim: c-Fos is often used as a proxy for neuronal firing.
source: Because c-Fos is often used as a proxy for neuronal firing, this result raises questions about the generalizability of RMTg responses to other aversive stimuli, albeit with the caveat that c-Fos likely reflects intracellular signaling events rather than firing per se (Kovács, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: c-Fos likely reflects intracellular signaling events rather than firing per se.
source: Because c-Fos is often used as a proxy for neuronal firing, this result raises questions about the generalizability of RMTg responses to other aversive stimuli, albeit with the caveat that c-Fos likely reflects intracellular signaling events rather than firing per se (Kovács, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: DA responses to aversive stimuli often exhibit a prominent inhibitory component.
source: Increasingly many studies have noted that DA responses to aversive stimuli, although somewhat complex, often exhibit a prominent inhibitory component (Fiorillo et al., 2013; Matsumoto et al., 2016; Tian and Uchida, 2015), and that the aversive stimulus-induced inhibition is associated with behavioral avoidance and diminished learning (Chang et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2018; Lammel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: Aversive stimulus-induced inhibition in DA neurons is associated with behavioral avoidance and diminished learning.
source: Increasingly many studies have noted that DA responses to aversive stimuli, although somewhat complex, often exhibit a prominent inhibitory component (Fiorillo et al., 2013; Matsumoto et al., 2016; Tian and Uchida, 2015), and that the aversive stimulus-induced inhibition is associated with behavioral avoidance and diminished learning (Chang et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2018; Lammel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: Inhibitory responses in DA neurons are primarily driven by GABAergic transmissions onto DA neurons.
source: Previous study has suggested that these inhibitory responses are primarily driven by GABAergic transmissions onto DA neurons (Henny et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citation.

claim: The sources of GABAergic transmissions onto DA neurons have been proposed to arise from numerous possible sources including the RMTg, lateral hypothalamus, ventral pallidum, extended amygdala, and GABAergic neurons in the VTA.
source: However, the sources of the GABAergic transmissions are still unknown, and have been proposed to arise from numerous possible sources including not only the RMTg, but also the lateral hypothalamus, ventral pallidum, extended amygdala, and GABAergic neurons in the VTA (Jennings et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: Out of 151 recorded neurons, 59 were located in the RMTg, as defined by immunostaining for FOXP1.
source: Out of 151 recorded neurons, 59 were located in the RMTg, as defined by immunostaining for FOXP1 (Lahti et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2018) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a methodological detail and result from the experiments.

claim: RMTg neurons on average showed significant inhibition to reward cues during a time window 200–400 ms post-stimulus.
source: Consistent with previous studies that RMTg neurons encode motivational valence (Hong et al., 2011; Jhou et al., 2009), we found that RMTg neurons on average showed significant inhibition to reward cues during a time window 200–400 ms post-stimulus, and rapid excitations to all other phasic stimuli 0–100 ms post-stimulus (p < 0.0001 for all stimuli) (Figure 2B; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: RMTg neurons showed rapid excitations to all phasic aversive stimuli 0–100 ms post-stimulus.
source: Consistent with previous studies that RMTg neurons encode motivational valence (Hong et al., 2011; Jhou et al., 2009), we found that RMTg neurons on average showed significant inhibition to reward cues during a time window 200–400 ms post-stimulus, and rapid excitations to all other phasic stimuli 0–100 ms post-stimulus (p < 0.0001 for all stimuli) (Figure 2B; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Responses to the three phasic aversive stimuli (footshock, siren, and bright light) were significantly greater than responses to the neutral tone.
source: Moreover, responses to the three phasic aversive stimuli (footshock, siren, and bright light) were significantly greater than responses to the neutral tone, suggesting an aversion-related augmentation in RMTg responses to aversive stimuli (F = 1.582, p = 0.027, p = 0.0001, and p = 0.0048 for neutral tone compared with footshock, siren, and bright light, repeated measures one-way ANOVA, Holm-Sidak test for multiple comparison) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 2.

claim: RMTg neuron response durations were largely confined to a period 0–100 ms after stimulus onset, independently of the total stimulus duration.
source: Notably, even though the duration of the aversive stimuli ranged from 10 ms up to 2 s, RMTg neuron response durations were largely confined to a period 0–100 ms after stimulus onset, independently of the total stimulus duration.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: 51% (30/59) of RMTg neurons showed significant changes relative to baseline firing to reward cue during a window 200–400 ms post-stimulus.
source: Specifically, we found 51% (30/59) of RMTg neurons showing significant changes relative to baseline firing (in either direction) to reward cue during a window 200–400 ms post-stimulus, with almost three-fourths of responsive neurons (22/30 = 73%) showing inhibition, and the remaining showing excitation.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from individual neuron analysis.

claim: Almost three-fourths of reward cue-responsive RMTg neurons (22/30 = 73%) showed inhibition.
source: Specifically, we found 51% (30/59) of RMTg neurons showing significant changes relative to baseline firing (in either direction) to reward cue during a window 200–400 ms post-stimulus, with almost three-fourths of responsive neurons (22/30 = 73%) showing inhibition, and the remaining showing excitation.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from individual neuron analysis.

claim: 59% (35/59), 70% (41/59), and 61% (36/59) of RMTg neurons showed significant changes from baseline firing to footshock, siren, and bright light during a window 0–100 ms post-stimulus.
source: Furthermore, 59% (35/59), 70% (41/59), and 61% (36/59) of RMTg neurons showed significant changes from baseline firing (in either direction) to footshock, siren, and bright light during a window 0–100 ms post-stimulus, again with roughly three-fourths showing excitations (24/35 = 68%, 31/41 = 75%, and 26/36 = 72% for footshock, siren, and light, respectively) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from individual neuron analysis.

claim: Roughly three-fourths of aversive stimulus-responsive RMTg neurons showed excitations (24/35 = 68%, 31/41 = 75%, and 26/36 = 72% for footshock, siren, and light, respectively).
source: Furthermore, 59% (35/59), 70% (41/59), and 61% (36/59) of RMTg neurons showed significant changes from baseline firing (in either direction) to footshock, siren, and bright light during a window 0–100 ms post-stimulus, again with roughly three-fourths showing excitations (24/35 = 68%, 31/41 = 75%, and 26/36 = 72% for footshock, siren, and light, respectively) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from individual neuron analysis.

claim: A majority (14/22) of reward cue-inhibited RMTg neurons showed significant excitations to footshock.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that a majority (14/22) of reward cue-inhibited neurons showed significant excitations to footshock, even though shock-excited neurons are only 41% of all RMTg neurons, indicating that shock-excitation patterns are particularly concentrated among the reward-cue inhibited population, contributing to an overall valence-encoding pattern in this population (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from individual neuron analysis.

claim: Among RMTg neurons significantly excited by footshock, responses were positively correlated with responses of each individual neuron to siren and bright light.
source: Moreover, among RMTg neurons significantly excited by footshock, these responses were positively correlated with responses of each individual neuron to siren and bright light, indicating that neurons more strongly activated by the footshock were also more strongly activated by siren and bright light (r2 = 0.2252, p = 0.004 and r2 = 0.1547, p = 0.0194 for siren and light respectively, 0–100 ms post-stimulus) (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from correlation analysis.

claim: Both LiCl (10 mg/kg i.p.) and restraint stress increased RMTg firing for several minutes after the onset of each stimulus.
source: We found that both LiCl (n = 22) and restraint stress (n = 12) increased RMTg firing for several minutes after the onset of each stimulus (first 0–10 min and 0–3 min post-stimulus, respectively, p = 0.01 and p = 0.02, repeated measure one-way ANOVA, Holm-Sidak test for multiple comparison).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: RMTg firing exhibited a 'rebound' inhibition to below baseline levels just after the offset of the aversive phases of LiCl and restraint stress.
source: Interestingly, RMTg firing exhibiting a 'rebound' inhibition to below baseline levels just after the offset of the aversive phases of each stimulus (20–30 min post-stimulus for LiCl and 9–12 min for restraint stress, p = 0.047, and p = 0.036, respectively, repeated measure one-way ANOVA, Holm-Sidak test for multiple comparison) (Figure 3A,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Saline injections of equal volume as the LiCl injections had no effect on RMTg firing.
source: In contrast, saline injections of equal volume as the LiCl injections had no effect on RMTg firing during either of the two time windows where LiCl had produced responses (n = 12, p = 0.23 and p = 0.84, respectively) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a control experiment result.

claim: Roughly 36–42% of RMTg neurons showed both an initial excitation and a rebound inhibition to LiCl and restraint stress.
source: Roughly 36–42% of RMTg neurons showed both an initial excitation and a rebound inhibition (8/22 and 5/12 neurons for LiCl and restraint stress, respectively), while the remaining neurons typically showed responses during only one of the two phases (Figure 3B,F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from individual neuron analysis.

claim: RMTg responses during the initial phase of LiCl and restraint stress were positively correlated with responses of these same neurons to footshock.
source: We found that RMTg responses during the initial phase of LiCl and restraint stress were positively correlated with responses of these same neurons to footshock (r2 = 0.1469, p = 0.0033 and r2 = 0.3783, p = 0.033, respectively) (Figure 3C,G), while their rebound inhibitory phase responses correlated with responses to reward cues (r2 = 0.2165, p < 0.0001 and r2 = 0.3954, p = 0.038, respectively) (Figure 3D,H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from correlation analysis.

claim: RMTg rebound inhibitory phase responses to LiCl and restraint stress correlated with responses to reward cues.
source: We found that RMTg responses during the initial phase of LiCl and restraint stress were positively correlated with responses of these same neurons to footshock (r2 = 0.1469, p = 0.0033 and r2 = 0.3783, p = 0.033, respectively) (Figure 3C,G), while their rebound inhibitory phase responses correlated with responses to reward cues (r2 = 0.2165, p < 0.0001 and r2 = 0.3954, p = 0.038, respectively) (Figure 3D,H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from correlation analysis.

claim: RMTg neurons were initially inhibited by cocaine 0–10 min post-infusion (initial phase), and subsequently activated 20–30 min post-infusion (rebound phase).
source: Specifically, they were initially inhibited by cocaine 0–10 min post-infusion (initial phase), and subsequently activated 20–30 min post-infusion (rebound phase), when cocaine was aversive (p = 0.0001 and p = 0.038, repeated measure one-way ANOVA, Holm-Sidak test for multiple comparison).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Saline infusions had no effect on RMTg firing during either initial or rebound phases.
source: Saline infusions (n = 14) had no effect on RMTg firing during either phase (p = 0.62 and p = 0.25) (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a control experiment result.

claim: 32% of RMTg neurons (12/38) exhibited both inhibition during the initial phase and excitation during the rebound phase of cocaine.
source: Furthermore, when individual neuron responses were analyzed, we found that 32% of RMTg neurons (12/38) exhibited both inhibition during the initial phase and excitation during the rebound phase, again consistent with the negative valence-encoding pattern seen previously (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from individual neuron analysis.

claim: RMTg responses during the initial phase of cocaine were positively correlated with responses to food-predictive cues.
source: Furthermore, responses during the initial phase were positively correlated with responses of these same neurons to food-predictive cues (r2 = 0.3267, p < 0.0001), while responses during the rebound phase were positively correlated with responses to footshocks (r2 = 0.1469, p = 0.003).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from correlation analysis.

claim: RMTg responses during the rebound phase of cocaine were positively correlated with responses to footshocks.
source: Furthermore, responses during the initial phase were positively correlated with responses of these same neurons to food-predictive cues (r2 = 0.3267, p < 0.0001), while responses during the rebound phase were positively correlated with responses to footshocks (r2 = 0.1469, p = 0.003).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from correlation analysis.

claim: Animals developed place aversion when placed into conditioning chambers immediately after LiCl injection (0-15 min).
source: In separate groups of LiCl-treated groups, we found that animals developed place aversion when placed into conditioning chambers immediately after the injection, but showed place preference when placed into chambers 15 min after the injection (p < 0.0001 and p = 0.02 for 0–15 min and 15–30 min, respectively) (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from conditioned place preference experiments.

claim: Animals showed place preference when placed into chambers 15 min after LiCl injection (15-30 min).
source: In separate groups of LiCl-treated groups, we found that animals developed place aversion when placed into conditioning chambers immediately after the injection, but showed place preference when placed into chambers 15 min after the injection (p < 0.0001 and p = 0.02 for 0–15 min and 15–30 min, respectively) (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from conditioned place preference experiments.

claim: Cocaine-treated animals developed place preference if conditioned immediately after infusion (0-15 min).
source: In contrast, separate groups of cocaine-treated animals developed place preference if conditioned immediately after infusion, and place aversion if conditioned 15 min later (p = 0.034 and p < 0.0001, respectively) (Figure 3O).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from conditioned place preference experiments.

claim: Cocaine-treated animals developed place aversion if conditioned 15 min after infusion (15-30 min).
source: In contrast, separate groups of cocaine-treated animals developed place preference if conditioned immediately after infusion, and place aversion if conditioned 15 min later (p = 0.034 and p < 0.0001, respectively) (Figure 3O).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from conditioned place preference experiments.

claim: Saline injections did not produce place preference during either time window.
source: Saline injections did not produce place preference during either time window (p = 0.412 and p = 0.562, respectively) (Figure 3P).
evidence: This is a control experiment result.

claim: VTA-projecting RMTg neurons were on average inhibited by reward cues and activated by footshocks.
source: We found that VTA-projecting neurons were on average inhibited by reward cues and activated by footshocks, that is a negative valence-encoding pattern (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Among 25 VTA-projecting RMTg neurons, a majority (14/25 neurons) were inhibited by reward cues and activated by footshocks.
source: Analysis of individual neurons further confirmed this; among 25 VTA-projecting neurons, a majority (14/25 neurons) were inhibited by reward cues and activated by footshocks, while 7/25 neurons responded to only one of the two stimuli, with the remaining four neurons showing no response to either stimulus.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from individual neuron analysis.

claim: Individual VTA-projecting RMTg neuron responses to reward cues correlated negatively with responses to footshocks.
source: Furthermore, individual neuron responses to reward cues correlated negatively with responses to footshocks (r2 = 0.2661, p = 0.0070) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from correlation analysis.

claim: DRN-projecting RMTg neurons on average showed no responses to reward cues.
source: In marked contrast to VTA-projecting neurons, DRN-projecting neurons on average showed no responses to reward cues, although there was an average activation by footshocks, similar to VTA-projecting neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: DRN-projecting RMTg neurons showed an average activation by footshocks.
source: In marked contrast to VTA-projecting neurons, DRN-projecting neurons on average showed no responses to reward cues, although there was an average activation by footshocks, similar to VTA-projecting neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: DRN-projecting RMTg neuron responses to reward cues and footshocks did not correlate with each other.
source: Analysis of individual neurons further showed that responses to reward cues and footshocks did not correlate with each other (p = 0.9775) (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from correlation analysis.

claim: VTA- and DRN-projecting RMTg neurons exhibited markedly different proportions of neurons that were inhibited by reward cues.
source: Overall, VTA- and DRN-projecting neurons exhibited markedly different proportions of neurons that were inhibited by reward cues (p = 0.001, Chi-square) (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical comparison.

claim: Putative dopamine neurons (pDA neurons) were classified by their phasic activations to reward cues.
source: We classified recorded VTA neurons as being putative dopamine neurons (pDA neurons) by their phasic activations to reward cues (Sham: n = 21 pDA, n = 45 non-pDA, Lesion: n = 17 pDA, n = 40 non-pDA, p < 0.05 during 0–200 ms after reward cues), an activity signature repeatedly shown to correlate highly with optogenetically identified DA neurons in mice (Cohen et al., 2012; Eshel et al., 2015; Matsumoto et al., 2016) (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is a methodological approach based on prior literature.

claim: About 1/3 of recorded VTA neurons in sham lesioned rats exhibited ramping activities in responses to reward cues.
source: We also observed about 1/3 of recorded VTA neurons in sham lesioned rats exhibiting ramping activities in responses to reward cues (p < 0.05 during 200–2000 ms after reward cue onset), which are consistent with firing patterns found in genetically identified GABAergic neurons in the VTA (Cohen et al., 2012; Eshel et al., 2015) (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from the data with reference to prior literature.

claim: Most pDA neurons in the sham group showed inhibitions to aversive stimuli, in some cases after a brief initial excitation.
source: We found that most pDA neurons in the sham group showed inhibitions to aversive stimuli, in some cases after a brief initial excitation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: 86% of stimulus-responsive pDA neurons were inhibited by footshock.
source: Specifically, 86% of stimulus-responsive pDA neurons were inhibited by footshock (54% showing only inhibition; 32% showing delayed inhibition after a brief initial excitation), 75% by siren (28% showing only inhibition; 47% showing delayed inhibition), and 56% by bright light (27% showing only inhibition; 29% showing delayed inhibition), while the remaining showed excitation only (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from individual neuron analysis.

claim: 75% of stimulus-responsive pDA neurons were inhibited by siren.
source: Specifically, 86% of stimulus-responsive pDA neurons were inhibited by footshock (54% showing only inhibition; 32% showing delayed inhibition after a brief initial excitation), 75% by siren (28% showing only inhibition; 47% showing delayed inhibition), and 56% by bright light (27% showing only inhibition; 29% showing delayed inhibition), while the remaining showed excitation only (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from individual neuron analysis.

claim: 56% of stimulus-responsive pDA neurons were inhibited by bright light.
source: Specifically, 86% of stimulus-responsive pDA neurons were inhibited by footshock (54% showing only inhibition; 32% showing delayed inhibition after a brief initial excitation), 75% by siren (28% showing only inhibition; 47% showing delayed inhibition), and 56% by bright light (27% showing only inhibition; 29% showing delayed inhibition), while the remaining showed excitation only (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from individual neuron analysis.

claim: Inhibition by aversive stimuli in pDA neurons was most prominent during a 100–500 ms window post-stimulus.
source: Notably, inhibition by aversive stimuli was most prominent during a 100–500 ms window post-stimulus, while activation by reward cues was most prominent in an earlier 0–200 ms window post-stimulus, a timing pattern opposite to that of RMTg neurons in which responses to aversive stimuli tended to be faster by a few hundred milliseconds (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: RMTg lesions did not affect the magnitude nor the percentage of VTA neurons responding to reward cues.
source: Among recorded VTA neurons, we found that RMTg lesions did not affect the magnitude nor the percentage of neurons responding to reward cues (0–200 ms post-stimulus) (p > 0.05, two-way ANOVA, Bonferroni test for multiple comparison, p = 0.879, Chi-square) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is a result from lesion experiments.

claim: After RMTg lesions, pDA neurons no longer showed an average inhibition to any of the three phasic aversive stimuli.
source: We found that, after RMTg lesions, pDA neurons no longer showed an average inhibition to any of the three phasic aversive stimuli (Figure 5F), and the proportions of pDA neurons inhibited by aversive stimuli were dramatically reduced to 19%, 16%, and 18% for footshock, siren, and bright light, respectively (p < 0.0001, p = 0.008, and p = 0.048, Chi-square, 100–500 ms post-stimulus) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from lesion experiments.

claim: The proportions of pDA neurons inhibited by aversive stimuli were dramatically reduced after RMTg lesions to 19%, 16%, and 18% for footshock, siren, and bright light, respectively.
source: We found that, after RMTg lesions, pDA neurons no longer showed an average inhibition to any of the three phasic aversive stimuli (Figure 5F), and the proportions of pDA neurons inhibited by aversive stimuli were dramatically reduced to 19%, 16%, and 18% for footshock, siren, and bright light, respectively (p < 0.0001, p = 0.008, and p = 0.048, Chi-square, 100–500 ms post-stimulus) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from lesion experiments.

claim: In intact animals, 59%, 42%, and 36% of VTA neurons showed significant inhibitions to footshock, siren, and bright light.
source: Specifically, in intact animals, 59%, 42%, and 36% of VTA neurons showed significant inhibitions to footshock, siren, and bright light, while in RMTg-lesioned rats, these proportions were reduced to 21%, 16%, and 9%, respectively (p = 0.005, p = 0.017, and p = 0.004, for footshock, siren, and bright light, respectively, Chi-square) (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: In RMTg-lesioned rats, the proportions of VTA neurons showing inhibitions were reduced to 21%, 16%, and 9% for footshock, siren, and bright light, respectively.
source: Specifically, in intact animals, 59%, 42%, and 36% of VTA neurons showed significant inhibitions to footshock, siren, and bright light, while in RMTg-lesioned rats, these proportions were reduced to 21%, 16%, and 9%, respectively (p = 0.005, p = 0.017, and p = 0.004, for footshock, siren, and bright light, respectively, Chi-square) (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from lesion experiments.

claim: RMTg lesions increased the magnitudes of initial excitations in pDA neurons to aversive stimuli.
source: As noted above, many pDA neurons that were inhibited by aversive stimuli did so after brief initial excitations, and RMTg lesions increased the magnitudes of these initial excitations relative to shams (p = 0.013, p = 0.021, and p = 0.009 for siren, shock, and bright light, respectively, unpaired t-test), without affecting the proportion of pDA neurons exhibiting them (p = 0.169, p = 0.328, and p = 0.126 for siren, shock, and bright light, respectively, Chi-square) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is a result from lesion experiments.

claim: RMTg lesions did not alter basal firing rates of pDA neurons.
source: Notably, RMTg lesions did not alter basal firing rates of pDA neurons (5.4 Hz vs 5.2 Hz, n = 23, p = 0.507, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a result from lesion experiments.

claim: RMTg lesions increased the percentage of spikes found in bursts of pDA neurons.
source: However, we did find that RMTg lesions increased the percentage of spikes found in bursts of pDA neurons (p = 0.014, unpaired t-test) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is a result from lesion experiments.

claim: Sham rats expressed a significant aversion to all tested stimuli, as measured by both time spent in, and entries into, the stimulus-paired versus unpaired chambers.
source: We found that on average, sham rats expressed a significant aversion to all stimuli, as measured by both time spent in, and entries into, the stimulus-paired versus unpaired chambers (time spent: p = 0.007, p < 0.0001, p = 0.039, and p = 0.05, number of entries: p = 0.014, p < 0.0001, p < 0.0001, and p = 0.05, respectively for siren, LiCl, bright light, and cocaine, z-score).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from conditioned place aversion experiments.

claim: RMTg lesions showed a significant main effect on time spent in paired chamber in conditioned place aversion tests.
source: A two-way ANOVA comparing lesioned versus sham groups then showed a significant main effect of lesion for time spent in paired chamber (p = 0.01) (Figure 6B), due to lesioned rats having a smaller bias away from the stimulus-paired chambers, compared to sham rats.
evidence: This is a result from lesion experiments.

claim: RMTg lesions produced a main effect on preference score as measured by entries in conditioned place aversion tests.
source: RMTg lesions produced a somewhat stronger effect on the preference score as measured by entries, with the two-way ANOVA again showing a main effect of lesion (p < 0.0001), with this effect also being significant for each stimulus (p = 0.027, p = 0.003, p = 0.021, and p = 0.043 for siren, LiCl, bright light, and cocaine, respectively) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from lesion experiments.

claim: The lesion group showed slightly greater overall locomotor activities measured by photobeam counts.
source: Although preference scores could be confounded if RMTg lesions produce extreme motoric disinhibition, we found this was not the case; in particular, while the lesion group showed slightly greater overall locomotor activities measured by photobeam counts (p = 0.02, unpaired t-test) (Figure 6D), lesion and sham groups did not show differences in total chamber entries prior to conditioning, suggesting that effects of RMTg lesions on locomotion were minor (p = 0.106, unpaired t-test) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a result from behavioral experiments.

claim: Lesion and sham groups did not show differences in total chamber entries prior to conditioning.
source: Although preference scores could be confounded if RMTg lesions produce extreme motoric disinhibition, we found this was not the case; in particular, while the lesion group showed slightly greater overall locomotor activities measured by photobeam counts (p = 0.02, unpaired t-test) (Figure 6D), lesion and sham groups did not show differences in total chamber entries prior to conditioning, suggesting that effects of RMTg lesions on locomotion were minor (p = 0.106, unpaired t-test) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a result from behavioral experiments.

claim: Aversive conditioning reduced total chamber entries for all stimuli in the sham group.
source: Interestingly, aversive conditioning reduced total chamber entries for all three stimuli in the sham group (p = 0.04, p = 0.0004, p = 0.001, p = 0.035 for siren, bright light, LiCl, and cocaine, respectively, paired t-test) (Figure 6F), but not the RMTg lesioned group (p = 0.34, p = 0.22, p = 0.01, p = 0.425 for siren, bright light LiCl, and cocaine, respectively, paired t-test) (Figure 6G), suggesting an overall inhibitory effect of aversive conditioning in normal rats that was not present in the lesioned group.
evidence: This is a result from behavioral experiments.

claim: Aversive conditioning did not reduce total chamber entries in the RMTg lesioned group.
source: Interestingly, aversive conditioning reduced total chamber entries for all three stimuli in the sham group (p = 0.04, p = 0.0004, p = 0.001, p = 0.035 for siren, bright light, LiCl, and cocaine, respectively, paired t-test) (Figure 6F), but not the RMTg lesioned group (p = 0.34, p = 0.22, p = 0.01, p = 0.425 for siren, bright light LiCl, and cocaine, respectively, paired t-test) (Figure 6G), suggesting an overall inhibitory effect of aversive conditioning in normal rats that was not present in the lesioned group.
evidence: This is a result from behavioral experiments.

claim: The RMTg plays a broad role in encoding aversion and driving VTA responses and behavior.
source: Together, our findings indicate a broad RMTg role in encoding aversion and driving VTA responses and behavior.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: RMTg responses to sustained stimuli exhibit opponent processing patterns consistent with opponent process theory.
source: These RMTg responses parallel actual reward and aversion as measured by conditioned place preference, and suggest possible neural substrates of the opponent process model proposed decades ago to describe the phenomenon that removal of a strong affective stimulus often produces an affective state in the opposite direction of the initial stimulus (Solomon and Corbit, 1973).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with reference to a theoretical framework.

claim: The dose of LiCl used (10 mg/kg) is relatively low compared to doses commonly used to induce conditioned taste aversions.
source: Notably, the dose of LiCl that we used is relatively low compared to the much higher doses commonly used to induce conditioned taste aversions, and is thought to produce modest aversive effects lasting only approximately 15 min (Tomasiewicz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a methodological note with citation.

claim: The RMTg is defined by dense FOXP1 expression.
source: Out of 151 recorded neurons, 59 were located in the RMTg, as defined by immunostaining for FOXP1 (Lahti et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2018) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is inferred from the use of FOXP1 staining to define the RMTg region.

claim: The RMTg is a major source of GABAergic input to VTA dopamine neurons.
source: We further found that valence-encoding RMTg neurons preferentially project to the DA-rich VTA versus other targets, and excitotoxic RMTg lesions greatly reduce aversive stimulus-induced inhibitions in VTA neurons, particularly putative DA neurons, while also impairing conditioned place aversion to multiple aversive stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the lesion effects on VTA inhibitions and the known GABAergic nature of RMTg neurons.

claim: RMTg neurons encode negative valence.
source: These patterns are consistent with broad encoding of negative valence in a subset of RMTg neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the response patterns.

claim: The RMTg influences VTA responses to aversive stimuli through GABAergic inhibition.
source: We further found that valence-encoding RMTg neurons preferentially project to the DA-rich VTA versus other targets, and excitotoxic RMTg lesions greatly reduce aversive stimulus-induced inhibitions in VTA neurons, particularly putative DA neurons, while also impairing conditioned place aversion to multiple aversive stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the GABAergic nature of RMTg neurons and the loss of VTA inhibitions after RMTg lesions.

claim: Cocaine produces rewarding effects for about 10 min followed by an aversive 'crash' beginning around 15 min post-injection.
source: Three additional stimuli were sustained: lithium chloride (LiCl), restraint stress, and cocaine, lasting for several minutes in duration (Figure 2A). Stimuli were chosen to represent distinct sensory modalities, whose aversive qualities had been noted previously (Ettenberg et al., 1999; Tzschentke, 2007; Winston et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: The RMTg expresses nociceptin and somatostatin peptides.
source: However, the RMTg also expresses a number of peptides (nociceptin and somatostatin) that could mediate slower responses (Jhou et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: VTA GABAergic neurons exhibit ramping activities in response to reward cues that remain activated until animals receive rewards.
source: However, a series of elegant studies from Uchida's group have recorded genetically identified GABAergic neurons in the VTA and show that they exhibit ramping activities in responses to reward cues and that they remain activated until animals receive rewards (Cohen et al., 2012; Eshel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of VTA GABA interneurons disrupts phasic DA responses to reward cues and results in sustained DA activation throughout the entire presentation of cues.
source: Furthermore, prior work noted that optogenetic inhibition of VTA GABA interneurons disrupts phasic DA responses to reward cues and results in a sustained DA activation throughout the entire presentation of cues (Eshel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citation.

claim: RMTg neurons convey different information onto DA neurons than VTA GABAergic neurons.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that RMTg neurons convey completely different information onto DA neurons than VTA GABAergic neurons, and potentially mediate distinct aspects of motivated behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of findings with prior literature.

claim: The primary deficit in RMTg-lesioned rats is one of impulse inhibition, rather than aversive processing per se.
source: This may be consistent with other studies in which we found deficits in the ability to inhibit behaviors associated with negative outcomes, suggesting that the primary deficit in RMTg-lesioned rats is one of impulse inhibition, rather than aversive processing per se (Elmer et al., 2019; Laurent et al., 2017; Sánchez-Catalán et al., 2017; Vento et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with reference to prior work.

claim: Relief of pain induces increased DAergic signaling in the nucleus accumbens and induces place preference.
source: Furthermore, previous studies have indicated an important DA role in opponent processing, as relief of pain induced increased DAergic signaling in the nucleus accumbens, and induces place preference which could be blocked by intra-VTA infusion of GABA agonists, while inhibition of mesolimbic dopamine system results in diminished relief learning (Becerra et al., 2013; Mayer et al., 2018; Navratilova and Porreca, 2014; Navratilova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: The opponent processing signals could be potentially driven by the RMTg through inhibiting and disinhibiting VTA DA neurons.
source: Our results suggest that the opponent processing signals could be potentially driven by the RMTg through inhibiting and disinhibiting VTA DA neurons (Bourdy et al., 2014; Jalabert et al., 2011; Lecca et al., 2011; Lecca et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings with citations.

claim: A delay of several hundred milliseconds from RMTg activation to DA inhibition may be mediated by peptides rather than ionic conductance.
source: Notably, we observed a delay of several hundred milliseconds from the bulk of the RMTg activation to the bulk of the DA inhibition, a delay that may seem rather long for a monosynaptic connection, and certainly longer than expected for ionic conductance. However, the RMTg also expresses a number of peptides (nociceptin and somatostatin) that could mediate slower responses (Jhou et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of delayed responses and the known expression of peptides in the RMTg.

claim: The RMTg is a predominant driver of VTA inhibition by aversive stimuli.
source: These electrophysiological findings, taken together with our behavioral effects on conditioned place test, show a broad RMTg role in processing aversive stimuli. The RMTg is activated by aversive stimuli of a remarkably wide range of modalities and timescales, is a predominant driver of VTA inhibition by such aversive stimuli, and also drives place aversion to these stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: The RMTg drives place aversion to aversive stimuli.
source: These electrophysiological findings, taken together with our behavioral effects on conditioned place test, show a broad RMTg role in processing aversive stimuli. The RMTg is activated by aversive stimuli of a remarkably wide range of modalities and timescales, is a predominant driver of VTA inhibition by such aversive stimuli, and also drives place aversion to these stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the discussion.

claim: 112 rats were used for these experiments in total.
source: In total, 112 rats were used for these experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: 95 rats completed conditioned place tests.
source: 95 rats completed conditioned place tests, 48 were for Figure 3 and 47 were for Figure 6, of these, 24 rats had RMTg lesions.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: 15 rats underwent RMTg recordings.
source: 15 rats underwent RMTg recordings, and eight underwent VTA recordings.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Eight rats underwent VTA recordings.
source: 15 rats underwent RMTg recordings, and eight underwent VTA recordings.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.
